The '''X17 particle''' ('''X17 boson''') is a [[hypothetical]] [[subatomic particle]] proposed by [[Attila Krasznahorkay]] and his colleagues to explain certain anomalous measurement results; these anomalous measurements are known as '''ATOMKI anomaly''' or '''beryllium''' ('''<sup>8</sup>Be''') '''anomaly''' or '''X17 anomaly'''.<ref name="ARX-20191023">{{cite arXiv |last1=Krasznahorkay |first1=A. 'fifth force' faces scrutiny |magazine=[[Quanta Magazine]] |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/new-boson-claim-faces-scrutiny-20160607/ |access-date=20 November 2019 |quote=A lab in Hungary has reported an anomaly that could lead to a physics revolution. But even as excitement builds, closer scrutiny has unearthed a troubling backstory.}}</ref> [[vector boson]] with a mass near {{val|17|u=MeV/c2}}{{r|IND-20191121}} — which is about 33 times heavier than an [[electron]], but still very light for a [[boson]]. This is where it gets the name "X17".<ref name=CERN-plot-thickens/>

<!--Draft Text for Wikipedia: -->The hypothesis originated from observations of unexpected wide-angle trajectories of electron-positron ({{math|e<sup>+</sup>e<sup>−</sup>}}) pairs produced during the nuclear transitions of excited [[Beryllium-8]] nuclei. Similar resonant behavior was later reported by the same team in experiments involving [[Helium-4]] and [[Carbon-12]] nuclei. If confirmed, the X17 particle could represent the force carrier for a previously unknown [[fifth force]] of nature, often described in theoretical models as a "protophobic" (proton-ignoring) vector boson.<ref name=CERN-plot-thickens/><ref name="ATOMKI_2023"/>

Because the X17 particle is not predicted by the [[Standard Model]] of particle physics, its existence would require significant extensions to current physical theories. It has garnered substantial interest as a potential "portal" to the [[dark sector]], offering a possible candidate for [[dark matter]] interactions and a potential solution to other outstanding physics mysteries, such as the [[Muon g-2|muon anomalous magnetic moment]].<ref name="ATOMKI_2023"/>

Multiple independent experiments worldwide—such as the NA64 experiment at [[CERN]], the MEG II experiment at the [[Paul Scherrer Institute]], and the PADME experiment at the [[Laboratori Nazionali di Frascati]]—have been searching for evidence of the X17 particle, with recent data placing increasingly stringent constraints on its allowed properties.<ref name="ATOMKI_2023"/>

== History ==
In 2015, Krasznahorkay and his colleagues at [[ATOMKI]], the Hungarian Institute for Nuclear Research, posited the existence of a new, light [[boson]] with a mass of about {{val|17|u=MeV/c2}} (about 33 times heavier than the [[electron]]).<ref name="Cartlidge2016">{{Cite journal |last=Cartlidge |first=Edwin |date=2016-05-25 |title=Has a Hungarian physics lab found a fifth force of nature? |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/nature.2016.19957 |journal=Nature |language=en |doi=10.1038/nature.2016.19957 |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In an effort to find a [[dark photon]], the team fired [[proton]]s at thin targets of [[lithium-7]], which created beryllium-8 [[atomic nucleus|nuclei]] in an excited state, which then decayed to the ground state and produced pairs of [[electron]]s and [[positron]]s.<ref name=PRL-20160126/> Excess decays were observed at an opening angle of 140° between the {{subatomic particle|link=yes|electron+}} and {{subatomic particle|link=yes|electron-}} particles and a combined energy of approximately {{val|17|u=MeV/c2}}. This indicated that a small fraction of the excited beryllium-8 might shed its excess energy in the form of a new particle. The result was successfully repeated by the team.{{r|IND-20191121}}

Feng et al. (2016)<ref name=Feng-2016/> proposed that a "protophobic" X&nbsp;boson, with a mass of {{val|16.7|u=MeV/c2}}, suppressed [[coupling (physics)|couplings]] to protons relative to [[neutron]]s and electrons at [[femtometre]] range, could explain the data. The force may explain the [[Anomalous magnetic dipole moment#Muon|{{mvar|g}}&nbsp;−&nbsp;2 muon anomaly]] and provide a dark matter candidate. {{As of|2019}}, several research experiments are underway to attempt to validate or refute these results.<ref name=Cartlidge2016/><ref name=Feng-2016>{{cite journal |author1=Feng, Jonathan L. |display-authors=etal |year=2016 |title=Protophobic fifth force interpretation of the observed anomaly in <sup>8</sup>Be nuclear transitions |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=117 |issue=7 |article-number=071803 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.117.071803 |pmid=27563952 |bibcode=2016PhRvL.117g1803F |s2cid=206279817 |arxiv=1604.07411 |url=https://zenodo.org/record/1059042}}</ref>

Krasznahorkay (2019)<ref name=ARX-20191023/> posted a [[preprint]] announcing that he and his team at ATOMKI had successfully observed the same anomalies in the decay of stable helium atoms as had been observed in beryllium-8, strengthening the case for the existence of the X17&nbsp;particle.<ref name=ARX-20191023/>

This was covered in [[science journalism]], focusing largely on the implications that the existence of the X17&nbsp;particle and a corresponding fifth force would have in the search for dark matter.<ref name=SA-20191120>{{cite news |last=McRae |first=Mike |date=20 November 2019 |title=Physicists claim they've found even more evidence of a new force of nature |website=ScienceAlert.com |url=https://www.sciencealert.com/physicists-claim-a-they-ve-found-even-more-evidence-of-a-new-force-of-nature |access-date=20 November 2019}}</ref><ref name=CNN-20191122>{{cite news |last=Prior |first=Ryan |date=22 November 2019 |title=A 'no-brainer Nobel Prize': Hungarian scientists may have found a fifth force of nature |website=[[CNN News]] |url=https://www.cnn.com/2019/11/22/world/fifth-force-of-nature-scn-trnd/index.html |access-date=22 November 2019}}</ref><ref name=TE-20191121>{{cite news |last=Malewar |first=Amit |date=21 November 2019 |title=Scientists may have discovered the fifth force of nature – It's not the first time researchers claim to have caught a glimpse of it |website=TechExplorist.com |url=https://www.techexplorist.com/scientists-discovered-fifth-force-nature/27946/ |access-date=23 November 2019}}</ref>

== Exploration ==
<!--Draft Text for Wikipedia: -->
The X17 particle is theorized to be a new, light neutral [[boson]] with a mass of approximately 17 [[Electronvolt|MeV]]/''c''<sup>2</sup>.<ref name="ATOMKI_2023">{{Cite journal |last1=Krasznahorkay |first1=Attila J. |last2=Krasznahorkay |first2=Attila |last3=Csatlós |first3=Margit |last4=Timár |first4=János |last5=Begala |first5=Marcell |last6=Krakó |first6=Attila |last7=Rajta |first7=István |last8=Vajda |first8=István |last9=Sas |first9=Nándor J. |date=2024-10-31 |title=An Update of the Hypothetical X17 Particle |journal=Universe |language=en |volume=10 |issue=11 |pages=409 |doi=10.3390/universe10110409 |doi-access=free |arxiv=2409.16300 |bibcode=2024Univ...10..409K |issn=2218-1997}}</ref> The exact [[spin (physics)|spin]] and [[parity (physics)|parity]] of the particle remain subjects of intense debate among theoretical physicists. Various phenomenological models have proposed the X17 as a vector, axial-vector, or pseudoscalar particle in order to remain consistent with both the observed kinematic anomalies and the stringent constraints imposed by historical accelerator data. 

Recent theoretical work has also explored the possibility that the X17 particle possesses chiral couplings to [[quark]]s. This chiral framework naturally produces both vector and axial-vector couplings—similar to the Standard Model [[Weak interaction|weak interactions]]—which may help reconcile the reported ATOMKI signals with other experimental limits.<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Fieg |first1=Max H. |title=The X17 with Chiral Couplings |date=2026-02-11 |eprint=2602.11263 |last2=Mäkelä |first2=Toni |last3=Tait |first3=Tim M. P. |last4=Toman |first4=Miša |class=hep-ph }}</ref>

=== Theoretical ===
Because a 17 MeV boson is not predicted by the Standard Model, its existence requires the introduction of new physical frameworks. The two primary categories of theories are "[[beyond the Standard Model]]" (BSM) extensions and novel interpretations of existing quantum phenomena.

==== Fifth force ====
The most prominent BSM interpretation posits that the X17 particle acts as a force-carrying gauge boson for a hypothetical [[fifth force]] of nature. Early models described this as a "protophobic" force, meaning the X17 particle would couple preferentially to [[neutron]]s and [[electron]]s while largely ignoring [[proton]]s.<ref name="darkSector">{{cite arXiv |last=Graziani |first=Marco |title=Light dark sector via thermal decays of Dark Matter: the case of a 17 MeV particle coupled to electrons |date=2026-03-01 |class=hep-ph |eprint=2602.17620 }}</ref> 

==== Dark sector ====
Furthermore, the X17 has been widely hypothesized to act as a "portal" mediator between ordinary matter and a hidden [[dark sector]]. In these frameworks, the X17 could play a crucial role in the thermal interactions and decays of [[dark matter]] candidates.<ref name=darkSector/>

==== QED meson theory ====
An alternative theoretical approach argues that the X17 is not a fundamentally new elementary particle, but rather a collective excitation within the framework of [[quantum electrodynamics]] (QED). Proponents of this theory suggest that unknown dynamics in the QED sector could allow a light quark and antiquark to become bound and confined, forming a highly stable, neutral "QED meson."<ref>{{cite journal|last=Wong |first=Cheuk-Yin |title=QED Meson Description of the Anomalous Particles at ∼17 and ∼38 MeV |journal=Universe |date=2024-04-10 |volume=10 |issue=4 |page=173 |doi=10.3390/universe10040173 |doi-access=free |arxiv=2401.04142 |bibcode=2024Univ...10..173W }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Koshelkin |first1=Andrew V. |last2=Wong |first2=Cheuk-Yin  |chapter=Dynamics of quarks and gauge fields in the lowest-energy states in QCD and QED |chapter-url=https://pos.sissa.it/414/302/pdf |title=41st International Conference on High Energy physics, 6-13 July, 2022, Bologna, Italy |date=June 15, 2023  |arxiv=2212.11749  |doi=10.22323/1.414.302 |doi-broken-date=4 March 2026 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2023chep.confE.302K }}</ref> Under this interpretation, the anomalous 17 MeV signals correspond to the invariant mass of this composite state rather than a new fundamental force carrier.

== Skepticism ==
{{update|section|date=October 2023|reason=are the articles still not peer-reviewed?}}
{{As of|2019|12|df=}}, the ATOMKI paper describing the particle has not been [[Peer review|peer reviewed]] and should therefore be considered preliminary.<ref>{{cite web |first=Mara |last=Johnson-Groh |date=2019-12-09 |title=Mysterious 'particle X17' could carry a newfound fifth force of nature, but most experts are skeptical |website=Live Science |url=https://www.livescience.com/fifth-force-could-exist.html |access-date=2019-12-09}}</ref> In late 2019, a follow-up paper was published in ''[[Acta Physica Polonica B]]''.<ref name="DOI-2019">{{cite journal |last1=Krasznahorkay |first1=A.J. |last2=Csatlós |first2=M. |last3=Csige |first3=L. |last4=Firak |first4=D. |last5=Gulyás |first5=J. |last6=Nagy |first6=Á. |last7=Sas |first7=N. |last8=Timár |first8=J. |last9=Tornyi |first9=T.G. |year=2019 |title=On the ''X''(17) light-particle candidate observed in nuclear transitions |journal=Acta Physica Polonica B |volume=50 |issue=3 |page=675 |doi=10.5506/APhysPolB.50.675 |bibcode=2019AcPPB..50..675K |s2cid=126936875 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Efforts by [[CERN]] and other groups to independently detect the particle have been unsuccessful so far.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Banerjee |first1=D. |last2=Burtsev |first2=V.E. |last3=Chumakov |first3=A.G. |last4=Cooke |first4=D. |last5=Crivelli |first5=P. |last6=Depero |first6=E. |last7=Dermenev |first7=A.V. |last8=Donskov |first8=S.V. |last9=Dusaev |first9=R.R. |last10=Enik |first10=T. |last11=Charitonidis |first11=N. |date=2018-06-08 |title=Search for a hypothetical 16.7&nbsp;MeV gauge boson and dark photons in the NA64 Experiment at CERN |journal=Physical Review Letters |lang=en |volume=120 |issue=23 |article-number=231802 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.120.231802 |pmid=29932721 |issn=0031-9007 |bibcode=2018PhRvL.120w1802B |arxiv=1803.07748 |s2cid=49380594}}</ref>

The ATOMKI group had claimed to find various other new particles earlier in 2016 but abandoned these claims later, without an explanation of what caused the spurious signals. The group has also been accused of [[cherry-picking]] results that support new particles while discarding [[null result]]s.<ref name=QM-20160607/><ref>{{cite magazine |last=Siegel |first=Ethan |date=26 November 2019 |title=This is why the 'X17' particle and a new, fifth force probably don't exist |magazine=Forbes |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/startswithabang/2019/11/26/this-is-why-the-x17-particle-and-a-new-fifth-force-probably-dont-exist/#7c58618f2e82 |access-date=2019-11-28}}</ref>

The X17 particle is not consistent with the [[Standard Model]], so its existence would need to be explained by another theory.<ref name=SA-20191209>{{cite magazine |last=O'Callaghan |first=Jonathan |date=2019-12-09 |title=Evidence of new X17 particle reported, but scientists are wary |magazine=[[Scientific American]] |lang=en |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/evidence-of-new-x17-particle-reported-but-scientists-are-wary/ |access-date=2019-12-09}}</ref>

<!--Draft Text for Wikipedia: -->Several dedicated experiments have recently tested the X17 hypothesis. In late 2024, the MEG II collaboration at the Paul Scherrer Institute published the results of a dedicated four-week data-taking run utilizing a magnetic spectrometer. Investigating the same <math>{}^{7}\text{Li}(p, e^+e^-){}^{8}\text{Be}</math> reaction as ATOMKI, MEG II found no significant signal for the X17 particle, setting stringent new limits on its branching ratios.<ref>{{cite arXiv |author1=The MEG II Collaboration |title=Search for the X17 particle in <sup>7</sup>Li(p,e<sup>+</sup>e<sup>−</sup>)) <sup>8</sup>Be processes with the MEG II detector |date=2024-11-12 |eprint=2411.07994 |last2=Afanaciev |first2=K. |last3=Baldini |first3=A. M. |last4=Ban |first4=S. |last5=Benmansour |first5=H. |last6=Boca |first6=G. |last7=Cattaneo |first7=P. W. |last8=Cavoto |first8=G. |last9=Cei |first9=F. |class=nucl-ex }}</ref> Conversely, the Positron Annihilation into Dark Matter Experiment (PADME) at the Frascati National Laboratory conducted a highly targeted resonance scan in 2025. By firing a positron beam at a fixed target and varying the center-of-mass energy between 16.4 and 17.4 MeV, they searched for the direct resonant production of the X17 (<math>e^+ e^- \to X17 \to e^+ e^-</math>). The collaboration utilized a "blind" analysis to prevent researcher bias. Upon unblinding, they reported a moderate event excess at roughly 16.90 MeV, which aligns closely with the expected mass of the X17, though it currently remains at a moderate statistical significance of about 2 standard deviations.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bossi |first1=F. |title=Search for a new 17 MeV resonance via e<sup>+</sup>e<sup>−</sup> annihilation with the PADME experiment |date=2026-02-24 |arxiv=2505.24797 |last2=Sangro |first2=R. De |last3=Giulio |first3=C. Di |last4=Meco |first4=E. Di |last5=Domenici |first5=D. |last6=Finocchiaro |first6=G. |last7=Foggetta |first7=L. G. |last8=Garattini |first8=M. |last9=Gianotti |first9=P. |journal=Journal of High Energy Physics |volume=2025 |issue=11 |article-number=7 |doi=10.1007/JHEP11(2025)007 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Kozhuharov |first=V. |title=Proceedings of 42nd International Conference on High Energy Physics — PoS(ICHEP2024) |chapter=Searching for the X17 with the PADME experiment |date=2025-10-30 |page=727 |doi=10.22323/1.476.0727 |doi-access=free |arxiv=2510.26258 }}</ref>

== Evolving theoretical models ==
Earlier models assumed X17 was a simple "dark photon" (a vector boson), but the theoretical framework to explain the X17 signal has evolved significantly as new constraints from particle physics experiments have emerged, therefore forcing theorists to develop more complex models.
=== Chiral and axial-vector couplings ===
Analyses of the Carbon-12 data have strongly disfavored a purely "vector" boson scenario. Instead, theorists propose that if X17 is a spin-1 particle, it likely possesses "chiral" or "axial-vector" couplings to quarks and leptons—similar to the Standard Model's weak force—to evade strict limits set by pion decay experiments.<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Mommers |first1=Cornelis J. G. |title=Constraining the axial-vector X17 interpretation with <sup>12</sup>C data |date=2024-06-12 |eprint=2406.08143 |last2=Vanderhaeghen |first2=Marc |class=hep-ph }}</ref><ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Fieg |first1=Max H. |title=The X17 with Chiral Couplings |date=2026-02-11 |eprint=2602.11263 |last2=Mäkelä |first2=Toni |last3=Tait |first3=Tim M. P. |last4=Toman |first4=Miša |class=hep-ph }}</ref>

=== The QED meson hypothesis ===
An alternative theoretical approach argues that X17 is not a new fundamental particle belonging to a "dark sector" at all. Physicist Cheuk-Yin Wong has proposed that the 17 MeV signal represents a previously unobserved "confined state" of Quantum Electrodynamics (QED)—essentially an isoscalar QED meson.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Wong |first=Cheuk-Yin |title=QED Meson Description of the Anomalous Particles at ∼17 and ∼38 MeV |journal=Universe |date=2024-04-10 |volume=10 |issue=4 |page=173 |doi=10.3390/universe10040173 |doi-access=free |arxiv=2401.04142 |bibcode=2024Univ...10..173W }}</ref>
=== Links to other anomalies ===
Some theorists suggest that an X17 vector boson with specific chiral couplings could simultaneously explain the ATOMKI anomalies, the long-standing Muon <math>a = \frac{g - 2}{2}</math> anomaly, and the muonic Lamb shift.<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Capolupo |first1=Antonio |title=The impact of the X17 boson on particle physics anomalies: muon anomalous magnetic moment, Lamb shift, W mass and dark charges |date=2024-10-02 |eprint=2410.01430 |last2=Quaranta |first2=Aniello |last3=Serao |first3=Raoul |class=hep-ph }}</ref>
